clinical_knowledge.topic: Clostridioides difficile Infection evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Clostridioides difficile Infection is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Immediate contact isolation precautions (soap and water hand hygiene essential as alcohol hand rubs do not kill spores), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe watery diarrhoea 8 times a day and lower abdominal cramping for 4 days

Key HPI features: 4-day history of explosive, watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea occurring 8-10 times per 24 hours, including nocturnal episodes. Accompanied by lower abdominal cramping, low-grade fever, and generalized weakness. Discharged from hospital 10 days ago after completing a 7-day course of oral co-amoxiclav for community-acquired pneumonia.

Objective/Exam findings: Check HR, BP (postural drop), skin turgor, mucous membranes. Abdominal exam: diffuse mild tenderness without peritonism. Stool test: urgent Clostridioides difficile toxin A/B enzyme immunoassay and glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen. Bloods: FBC (leukocytosis common), renal profile (acute kidney injury check).
Relevant background/PMH: COPD, mild benign prostatic hyperplasia, recent pneumonia hospitalization
Current medications: tamsulosin 400mcg OD, tiotropium inhaler OD, recently completed co-amoxiclav course
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Clostridioides difficile Infection.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea without colitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Signs of dehydration (dry mouth, weakness) with high stool frequency — risk of severe colitis.
management_principles: Immediate contact isolation precautions (soap and water hand hygiene essential as alcohol hand rubs do not kill spores)
Initiate oral vancomycin 125mg QDS or oral fidaxomicin 200mg BD for 10 days
Avoid anti-motility agents (loperamide) due to risk of toxic megacolon
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Clinical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 71M post-antibiotic exposure presents with profuse watery diarrhoea (8-10x/day), abdominal cramping, and signs of dehydration.
reference_soap.objective: Check HR, BP (postural drop), skin turgor, mucous membranes. Abdominal exam: diffuse mild tenderness without peritonism. Stool test: urgent Clostridioides difficile toxin A/B enzyme immunoassay and glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen. Bloods: FBC (leukocytosis common), renal profile (acute kidney injury check).
reference_soap.assessment: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) secondary to recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use. DDx: antibiotic-associated diarrhoea without colitis, acute infectious gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Campylobacter), ischaemic colitis.
reference_soap.plan: Immediate contact isolation precautions (soap and water hand hygiene essential as alcohol hand rubs do not kill spores). Initiate oral vancomycin 125mg QDS or oral fidaxomicin 200mg BD for 10 days. Avoid anti-motility agents (loperamide) due to risk of toxic megacolon. IV crystalloid fluid rehydration and electrolyte correction.

learning_objectives: Link recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure directly to dysbiosis and C. difficile proliferation
Emphasize critical infection control mandates including mandatory soap-and-water handwashing over alcohol gel
Explain the contraindication of anti-motility agents in toxin-producing bacterial colitis
Assess volume depletion and acute kidney injury risk in elderly patients with profuse diarrhoea

teaching.one_liner: Antibiotics wipe out normal gut bacteria, letting C. difficile overgrow and release toxins that cause explosive, foul-smelling watery diarrhoea.
red_flags: Signs of dehydration (dry mouth, weakness) with high stool frequency — risk of severe colitis

must_ask.say: What antibiotics did you take recently, and when did you finish the course?
How many times a day are you going, and is it watery and foul-smelling?
Does it wake you up at night to go?
Have you had a fever with this?
Does your mouth feel dry, or are you feeling weak and dizzy?
Have you been in hospital recently?
Does anyone else at home have similar symptoms?

history.answer: I have been having terrible watery diarrhoea eight to ten times a day and lower stomach cramping for the past four days.
It started suddenly four days ago and has been non-stop and getting worse since then.
I run to the toilet eight to ten times every single day; it is completely liquid, explosive, and smells unusually foul.
No, I haven't noticed any red blood or dark black tarry material in the stool, just pure watery brown liquid.
Yes, it wakes me up two or three times during the night with an urgent need to run to the toilet.
I have dull, cramping pain across my lower belly that comes and goes; passing stool gives me slight relief, but only for a brief moment.
Yes, whenever I feel the urge, it is overwhelming, and I often feel like I haven't completely emptied my bowels.
I have felt warm and feverish over the last few days, and my home thermometer showed around thirty-eight degrees Celsius.
I feel a bit sick to my stomach from all the cramping, but I haven't actually thrown up.
My mouth feels like sandpaper and I feel dizzy whenever I stand up; my urine has also become very dark and small in volume.
I haven't eaten any raw seafood, unpasteurized milk, or buffet food, and my wife eats the exact same meals at home and has no symptoms at all.
No, I haven't traveled anywhere, gone camping, or drunk any untreated water from streams or wells.
I was admitted to the hospital ten days ago for pneumonia and stayed on the respiratory ward for several days.
Yes, while I was in the hospital and when I came home, I took a full seven-day course of co-amoxiclav antibiotic pills for my pneumonia.
I think I might have caught some kind of hospital superbug or bowel infection while I was admitted for my chest infection.
I am really worried that I am severely dehydrated and that my kidneys might be failing because my mouth is bone-dry and I'm hardly peeing.
I was hoping you could give me intravenous fluids to rehydrate me and the right antibiotic tablets to kill this bowel infection.
I haven't weighed myself this week, but I have not had any unintentional weight loss before this sickness started.
No, it doesn't change whether I drink milk or eat bread; the watery diarrhea happens regardless of what I eat.
No, I haven't been under any unusual stress, and I have never had alternating diarrhea and constipation before.
No, I don't have any aching joints, skin rashes, mouth ulcers, or red inflamed eyes.
No, I have not had heart palpitations, heat intolerance, or facial flushing.
I have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and mild prostate enlargement, and of course that recent bout of pneumonia.
I have never had any surgeries; my only recent stay was ten days ago for the pneumonia.
I take tamsulosin once a day for my prostate and use a tiotropium inhaler once daily for my lungs.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I used to smoke a pack a day for thirty years, but I quit twelve years ago.
I only have an occasional small beer on weekends, but I haven't had a single drop since getting sick.
I am a retired engineer and live in an apartment with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure, but nobody in my family has ever had Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or bowel cancer.

exam.finding: Elderly gentleman appearing weak and moderately dehydrated, but alert and oriented.
Blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
Supine blood pressure 108/68 mmHg with pulse 98 beats/min; standing blood pressure drops to 96/58 mmHg with pulse increasing to 114 beats/min.
Dry oral mucosa, cracked lips, and dry tongue with no oral aphthae or pharyngeal erythema.
Decreased skin turgor with slow recoil on the subclavicular area; capillary refill time prolonged at approximately 3 seconds.
Tachycardic regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 without audible cardiac murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Slightly prolonged expiratory phase with baseline coarse breath sounds, but no focal crackles or wheezing.
Abdomen is symmetric and flat without visible distension, peristaltic waves, or surgical scars.
Hyperactive, frequent, high-pitched bowel sounds auscultated across all four quadrants.
Tympanitic note throughout all abdominal quadrants without shifting dullness.
Mild diffuse tenderness over the lower abdomen, most prominent in the lower quadrants, without involuntary guarding or muscular rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited; abdominal wall remains soft on release.
Normal perianal skin without fissures, normal sphincter tone, and liquid foul-smelling brown stool without gross blood on the glove.
